name: Women Who Changed Science
description: From Hypatia in Alexandria to the Nobel winners of today, women who made major discoveries, often against the odds and without the credit they deserved.

checkpoints.name: Before the doors opened
checkpoints.note: Hypatia teaches in Alexandria, and centuries later Émilie du Châtelet and Caroline Herschel find ways to do real science in a world that kept women out of universities and societies.

checkpoints.name: The long century
checkpoints.note: Mary Anning digs fossils, Mary Somerville explains science to the public, Ada Lovelace imagines what a computer could do and Sofya Kovalevskaya wins a professorship in mathematics.

checkpoints.name: Labs and observatories
checkpoints.note: Marie Curie wins two Nobel Prizes, Leavitt measures the stars, Noether proves a deep link between symmetry and physics and Meitner explains fission, while many women still work without a proper title.

checkpoints.name: The double helix era
checkpoints.note: Franklin's X-rays help reveal DNA, and Wu, McClintock, Hodgkin, Carson and Goodall change physics, genetics, chemistry, ecology and primatology. Bell Burnell finds pulsars, Rubin finds evidence of dark matter, Tu Youyou finds a malaria drug, Tereshkova and Ride fly in space, and Hopper and Johnson shape computing.

checkpoints.name: New frontiers
checkpoints.note: Recognition catches up. Tu Youyou wins a Nobel Prize in 2015 for her malaria drug, Mirzakhani becomes the first woman to win the Fields Medal in 2014, and Doudna helps invent CRISPR gene editing, winning the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
